question.leadin: China wasn't the only country that built great walls.
question.text: This Roman emperor built a namesake wall to mark the northern boundary of Roman Britain. He also suppressed the Bar Kokhba revolt in Judea.
question.clue: This ruler commissioned the massive Temple of Venus and Rome after exiling his predecessor's architect Apollodorus of Damascus.

swap.leadin: Answer the following about the real-life Roman namesakes of the Gamemakers from The Hunger Games.
swap.text: The Gamemaker Seneca Crane shares his name with Seneca the Younger, the tutor of this Roman Emperor. This man allegedly played a fiddle during the Great Fire of Rome.
swap.answerHtml: Nero Claudius Caesar Augustus Germanicus [accept Lucius Domitius Ahenobarbus]
swap.clue: This ruler built a boat designed to sink to kill his mother, Agrippina the Younger, who opposed his relationship with Poppaea Sabina .

question.text: The loss at Cannae triggered a change in Roman strategy, leading to final victory in this war at the Battle of Zama.
question.clue: After losing their Celtic allies to a bribe, the brothers Publius and Gnaeus Scipio were defeated at the Battles of the Upper Baetis during this war.

swap.leadin: To complete this siege, attacking forces built a wall around a hilltop fort, then built a wall around themselves to protect from a reinforcing army.
swap.text: Name this 52 BCE siege of a hilltop fort commanded by Vercingetorix, whose surrender essentially guaranteed the fall of Gaul.
swap.clue: Prior to this battle, a council held at Bibracte united the force of one side, which led their opponent to mount a failed attack at the hill of Gergovia.

question.leadin: Answer the following about leisure in ancient Rome.
question.text: When Romans exercised it was usually at the palestra, the exercise ground at these places. These places, which included rooms like the frigidarium and caldarium, were known in Latin as thermae.
question.clue: One example of these buildings in Britain was dedicated to the goddess Sulis, while examples of these buildings in Rome were named after Caracalla and Diocletian.

swap.leadin: Answer the following about the 216 BC Battle of Cannae ("kan-AY").
swap.text: The losing Roman side during the Battle of Cannae included Lucius Aemilius Paullus and Gaius Tarentius Varro, who were two people who held this position. This highest executive position in the Roman Republic was led by two people at once.
swap.clue: Lucius Junius Brutus was the first holder of this position, while Caligula tried to elevate his horse Incitatus to this position and Gaius Marius held it for an unprecedented seven terms.

question.leadin: This man's wife drove over her dead father's body with a chariot in a road now known as the "Street of Crime."
question.text: Name this man who usurped Servius Tullius to become king of Rome. He himself was popularly overthrown after his son Sextus raped a woman named Lucretia.
question.answerHtml: Tarquin the Proud (or Lucius Tarquinius Superbus; prompt on Lucius Tarquinius)
question.clue: This last king of Rome was legendarily deposed and exiled after his son Sextus raped Lucretia, the wife of Lucius Collatinus.

swap.text: In this century-long sequence of wars Rome fought Carthage for the control of the Mediterranean.
swap.clue: The second of these conflicts was started after the Siege of Saguntum, and one side in these conflicts employed the Fabian Strategy.

question.text: Androgynous priests known as Galli facilitated the worship of this Roman cult deity. Priests bathed in bull's blood to honor this mother goddess, whose cult became popular during the Second Punic War.

swap.leadin: Answer the following about people who may have come from Lydia or Umbria.
swap.text: This Italian civilization, which was eventually absorbed by the Romans, had no centralized government. Instead, it was comprised of a loose Confederation of cities like Clusium and Veii.
swap.clue: The names of gods in this language are on a sheep liver-shaped bronze artifact used for haruspicy found at Piacenza.

question.leadin: Answer the following about Roman occupation of Britain.
question.text: As governor of Britannia, this Roman general subdued the Caledonians and Ordovices, winning the battle of Mons Graupius in Scotland. Father-in-law of Tacitus, he was recalled by Domitian, but not before he circumnavigated Britain.
question.clue: He served under Salvius Titianus after being appointed quaestor in Asia and after he shared a battle tent with his military tutor Suetonius Paulinus.

swap.leadin: This structure stretched 73 miles from Wallsend-on-Tyne to Solway Firth.
swap.text: Identify this structure that was built by the Romans as a defense mechanism against barbarians in England. Begun in AD 122, its namesake emperor also dealt with the Bar Kokhba revolt in Judea.
swap.clue: A birthday invitation was found on one of the Vindolanda tablets, which were unearthed near this structure.

question.leadin: Viriathus led a rebellion that Polybius called the "fiery war" in this region, where velites ("WAY-lee-tace") units failed to counter weapons like the pilum ("PEE-loom") and falcata in the Numantine War.
question.text: Identify this region that contained the mysterious Tartessos civilization. After Sulla's civil war, Quintus Sertorius led a revolt in this region, where "New Carthage" controlled rich silver mines before the Battle of Ilipa ("ILL-ipp-uh").
question.answerHtml: Hispania [accept Iberia or Iberian peninsula; accept Spain or España; accept Portugal; accept Catalonia or Catalunya; accept Hispania Baetica or Hispania Tarraconensis or Hispania Citerior or Hispania Ulterior; accept Lusitania or Lusitanian War; accept Andalusia or Andalucía; accept Murcia] (“New Carthage” is Cartagena.)
question.clue: This region was once divided into provinces termed "Citerior" and "Ulterior."

swap.leadin: Answer some questions about the Roman Empire's conquest of the Balkans.
swap.text: Roman rule over the northwest Balkans came after they conquered these people, whose queen Teuta ruled the Ardiaei kingdom. Many later Roman Emperors like Constantine I were ethnically part of these people.
swap.clue: Before dying at Cannae, Lucius Aemilius Paullus forced these people to surrender Issa, held by Demetrius of Pharos, ending their namesake second war.

question.text: This saint asked, "if Rome can perish, what can be safe?" in a letter written during the invasion. His letters to St. Marcella, who died in Rome during the sack, are the best known sources for her life.

swap.text: This king of Clusium had his invasion of Rome repelled by the heroic actions of Horatius Cocles on the Pons Sublicius, as immortalised in a poem by T. B. Macaulay.
swap.clue: This figure was saved from death when a would-be assassin mistook his scribe for him, and that assassin thrust his right hand into a fire in an act of defiance against this figure.

question.text: Name this speech which was written to acquit its title politician of the murder of Clodius.
question.clue: This defense oration which becamse known in published form, composed for the Optimate rival of Julius Caesar, who was charged with murder following an incident at Bovillae.

swap.leadin: This man received his most famous name after being forced to thrust his right hand into some flaming coals.
swap.text: Identify this legendary soldier who carried out the aforementioned task without flinching and afterward received his sword into his left hand.
swap.clue: Captured while trying to assassinate the Etruscan king, this man thrust his right hand into a fire in order to demonstrate Roman bravery, scaring the Etruscans into a truce.

question.leadin: This man's opinions, along with those of Gaius, Papinian, Modestinus, and Paulus, were made legally authoritative by the incredibly phoned-in Law of Citations issued by Galla Placidia.
question.text: Name this Roman jurist of the Severan dynasty who authored influential commentaries such as Ad Sabinum and Ad Edictum.

swap.leadin: Answer the following about the pathetic career of co-emperor Lucius Verus.
swap.text: Just a couple years into the Marcomannic Wars, Verus croaked of food poisoning at the start of this plague that ran from 165 to 180 AD, and is sometimes named in honor of Galen.
